episodes.210980: A front moving through brought a squall line through western Massachusetts and into central Massachusetts producing pockets of damaging winds which downed several trees.
episodes.210995: An MCV approaching from the Upper Ohio Valley began tracking into Ohio during the late afternoon and evening hours where a more favorable environment over western and central Pennsylvania allowed for a cluster of severe thunderstorms. Ample shear in the realm of 40 to 50 knots, CAPE values between 1000 to 1500 J/kg, and increasing low-level moisture allowed for an increase in severe potential as thunderstorms entered central Pennsylvania during the evening hours. An initial cluster of thunderstorms began to split the border between New York and Pennsylvania, with ample low-level shear allowing for broad rotation within these storms. Multiple instances of tree damage were observed in McKean County, with an observed 60 mph wind gust in Potter County. A secondary cluster of thunderstorms later in the evening caused isolated tree damage in both Cameron County and Elk County. This cluster of thunderstorms weekend slightly downwind of the Allegheny Plateau, moving through sparsely populated areas of northern Clinton, northern Lycoming, Potter, and Tioga counties before moving into eastern Lycoming County. In eastern Lycoming County, multiple instances of damage to structures were reported north of Williamsport with multiple instances of tree damage observed before thunderstorms shifted east of the region.
episodes.210996: A remnant cluster of showers and weakening thunderstorms produced localized gale-force winds over the upper Chesapeake Bay during the late evening hours.
episodes.211025: Showers and thunderstorms developed along a stalled out frontal boundary that was situated across the Ohio Valley.
episodes.211088: On the evening of April 15th, a line of thunderstorms tracking east over Lake Erie intensified as they tracked onshore into northwestern Pennsylvania, Chautauqua County and Southern Erie County. As the storms continued east they became severe, causing two tornadoes in Cattaraugus County along with damaging wind gusts across a large chunk of the Western Southern Tier. The thunderstorms were associated with a Mesoscale Convective Vortex, that per usual for these types of setups, had plenty of shear to support the development of a tornado or two. Due to the lower instability values along with showers and increased cloud cover ahead of and behind the primary line, additional thunderstorms weren't able to develop.
episodes.211232: A round of moderate to heavy rain developed during the evening hours on Tuesday (4/14) north of a semi-stationary front located across southern Wisconsin. Rainfall amounts of 1 to 2 inches in a short period of time, combined with heavy rainfall the previous night, caused additional flash flooding across portions of central and east-central Wisconsin.
episodes.211298: Similar to previous days, a few thunderstorms developed off of a dryline across the Permian Basin and Big Bend/Lower Trans-Pecos. One storm produced severe winds in Big Spring (gusting up to 60 mph).
episodes.211376: Scattered thunderstorms moved across most of far northern Illinois during the evening of April 14th producing large hail, wind damage.  Flash flooding also occurred in parts of the Chicago metro area.
episodes.211377: Scattered thunderstorms moved across southern Lake Michigan during the evening of April 14th into the early morning of April 15th.
episodes.211378: Isolated severe thunderstorms produced flooding and marginally severe hail in the early morning of April 15th across far northern Illinois.  Scattered thunderstorms moved across most of northern Illinois during the evening of April 15th producing localized wind damage, hail and flooding.
episodes.211654: During the afternoon and evening hours of April 15th, severe storms brought very large hail and damaging wind gusts to portions of far eastern Kansas.
episodes.211676: During the afternoon and evening hours of April 15th, severe storms brought all severe hazards to portions of Missouri.
episodes.211765: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and central Oklahoma and north Texas from the evening of the 14th into early morning hours of the 15th. Despite strong wind shear and instability, residual low-level inhibition (i.e. cap), limited overall storm organization and longevity. The most notable thunderstorm impacted portions of Elk City, Oklahoma (and vicinity), producing large hail and significant wind gusts.
episodes.211766: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and central Oklahoma and north Texas on the evening of the 14th. Despite strong wind shear and instability, residual low-level inhibition (i.e. cap), limited overall storm organization and longevity. The most notable thunderstorm impacted portions of eastern Foard County, producing reports of large hail.
episodes.211767: Numerous severe thunderstorms, including supercells, developed along a trailing frontal boundary from western-north Texas into north-central Oklahoma on the afternoon into evening of the 15th. The strongest storms produced large to very large hail and sporadic damaging wind reports. Repeated thunderstorm activity across southeastern Oklahoma also led to localized flooding here.
episodes.211768: Numerous severe thunderstorms, including supercells, developed along a trailing frontal boundary from western-north Texas into north-central Oklahoma on the afternoon into evening of the 15th. The strongest storms produced large to very large hail and sporadic damaging wind reports.
episodes.211785: Several severe storms developed across portions of western Wisconsin during the late afternoon hours on April 14th and produced severe hail in many locations. The most notable of these storms developed over Vernon County, where wind-driven baseball-sized hail caused significant damage in the town of Westby, WI. This resulted in over $20 million USD in damage to the town and surrounding areas per input from Vernon County emergency management. Most homes received significant roof, siding, and window damage. As this storm moved eastward towards Juneau County, it also produced an intense EF-3 tornado near the town of Union Center where a home was leveled to its foundation.
episodes.211799: Supercell thunderstorms which developed along a dryline produced several instances of large hail and isolated damaging winds as they moved through western and northwestern portions of North Texas the evening of April 15.
episodes.211896: Severe storms moved across the Ozarks from April 14 to 15, 2026, and brought intense multi-hazard weather. The system advanced in two primary waves driven by escalating atmospheric instability. Unseasonably warm air pushed temperatures into the mid-80s. Strong southern winds gusted between 30 and 40 mph, injecting high humidity into the region. The initial round of storms were discrete supercell thunderstorms which formed over the Ozark Plateau. These initial isolated cells primarily produced large hail. The storms then developed into a training complex which brought heavy downpours. Total rainfall accumulated between 1 and 4 inches, triggering flash flooding and rapid rises in local streams.
episodes.211902: Strong to severe storms developed rapidly in the late afternoon into evening hours with initial supercells developing into a squall line.  The system was fueled by warm, humid Gulf air ahead of a front which brought widespread 60+ mph wind gusts, torrential flash flooding and large hail.
episodes.211938: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed over central Oklahoma during the early evening of the 14th, ahead of a dry line and an approaching upper level disturbance. The thunderstorms moved eastward into eastern Oklahoma during the late evening as they organized into a squall line. The line of thunderstorms produced several tornadoes and damaging wind.||Another round of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across portions of eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 15th. The strongest thunderstorms produced large hail up to two inches in diameter and damaging wind.
episodes.211939: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed over central Oklahoma during the early evening of the 14th, ahead of a dry line and an approaching upper level disturbance. The thunderstorms organized into a squall line and moved eastward into northwestern Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 15th. The line of thunderstorms produced several tornadoes and damaging wind.||Another round of strong to severe thunderstorms developed into northwestern Arkansas during the evening of the 15th. The strongest thunderstorms produced damaging wind.
episodes.212188: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
episodes.212318: On Tuesday, April 14th, a southwest flow pattern transported a warm, humid air mass into central New York, creating a favorable environment for severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening. The combination of sufficient instability, strong wind shear, and an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary ingredients for thunderstorm development. The strongest storms produced estimated damaging wind gusts of 50 knots knocking down trees and wires.
episodes.212390: Significant severe storms on the afternoon and evening of April 14th brought numerous reports of large hail, damaging wind, and multiple tornadoes.  The U.S. Hwy 20 corridor saw a long lived supercell that producing large hail (up to baseball size), damaging wind (88 mph gust at the Dubuque Airport), and several tornadoes.  Additional storms developed further south between I-80 and Hwy 20 that brought large hail and a photogenic tornado near Onslow, IA.  ||More storms quickly followed overnight and again on the next day, April 15th, bringing heavy rain, large hail, and isolated wind damage. Rainfall amounts over 1.5 were common north of I-80, with the highest totals over 3.5 seen in northwest IL.  This caused a mudslide on Hwy 84 in Carroll County closing the road for an extended period of time.
episodes.212391: Significant severe storms on the afternoon and evening of April 14th brought numerous reports of large hail, damaging wind, and multiple tornadoes.  The U.S. Hwy 20 corridor saw a long lived supercell that producing large hail (up to baseball size), damaging wind (88 mph gust at the Dubuque Airport), and several tornadoes. episodes.212432: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin in the evening hours of April 14th and eventually merged into line of storms as it tracked across southeastern WI before pushing out over Lake Michigan producing widespread strong winds.
episodes.212449: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms swept across central and southern Lower Michigan from late in the evening of April 14 to early in the morning on April 15, 2026. These storms packed very strong winds, spawning 5 tornadoes across Southeast MI as well as numerous instances of straight-line wind damage.
episodes.212451: At the surface, a cold front moved southward across central Lower MI and southern ON toward southern Lower MI and southwestern NY during the evening of the 13th. Ahead of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across northwest OH during the early evening hours and generated small to marginally-severe hail and isolated straight-line convective wind damage amidst moderate effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.||During the 14th, the aforementioned front shifted back northward to central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and near Lake Ontario, and then wavered in vicinity of those areas through the early afternoon of the 15th as multiple, weak surface lows moved generally eastward along the front. South of the front, northern OH resided in the warm and relatively-moist sector. Within this sector, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across portions of northern OH during the early afternoon of the 14th. This line of storms generated isolated straight-line convective wind damage via an outflow surge in Greenwich, Huron County, OH. Then, during the early evening of the 14th, a cluster of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally east-northeastward and produced hail up to the size of quarters to ping pong balls in northeastern Crawford and northern Richland Counties, OH. All of these storms occurred in an ambient environment with moderate MUCAPE and effective bulk shear, respectively.||During the rest of the afternoon through early evening of April 15th, the aforementioned front continued to waver in vicinity of central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and Lake Ontario as multiple and weak surface lows continued to move generally eastward along the front. South of the front, scattered multicell and supercell thunderstorms developed and persisted generally eastward in the warm/moist sector in northern OH. The storms produced severe hail and damaging straight-line wind gusts amidst an ambient environment with primarily moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. These storms included a prolific supercell that produced sporadic large hail in portions of Cuyahoga, Geauga, and Trumbull Counties, and likely caused millions of dollars in hail-related damage.
episodes.212452: At the surface, a cold front moved southward across central Lower MI and southern ON toward southern Lower MI and southwestern NY during the evening of the 13th. Simultaneously and ahead (i.e. south) of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward and produced sporadic peak straight-line convective wind gusts of gale-to-storm-force along the OH shore amidst moderate effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.||During the 14th, the aforementioned front shifted back northward to central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and near Lake Ontario, and then wavered in vicinity of those areas through the early afternoon of the 15th as multiple, weak surface lows moved generally eastward along the front. Within the warm and relatively-moist sector south of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward over and near Lake Erie and generated sporadic gale-force peak straight-line convective wind gusts along the OH shore during the predawn hours of the 15th amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.
episodes.212489: During the late evening and overnight hours of April 14th, 2026, a surge of low-level moisture moved northward into the region. This influx, combined with steep mid-level lapse rates and strong, highly unidirectional wind shear, generated an environment favorable for severe organized convection.||Widely scattered strong to severe thunderstorms subsequently developed and tracked across the area during the late evening. The storms produced multiple reports of quarter-sized hail (one inch in diameter), including a report from a trained weather spotter in Beatrice, NE at 9:17 PM CST, and another from Emergency Management in Essex, IA at 10:27 PM CST.||In addition to the hail threat, repeated rounds of storms trained over the same areas, producing localized heavy rainfall across portions of southeast Nebraska. This training behavior prompted the issuance of two Flash Flood Warnings covering Gage, Johnson, and Otoe counties, where radar imagery estimated localized rainfall totals of 2.00 to 3.50 inches within a few hours. Despite the heavy downpours, no flash flooding impacts were reported.
episodes.212490: During the late evening and overnight hours of April 14th, 2026, a surge of low-level moisture moved northward into the region. This influx, combined with steep mid-level lapse rates and strong, highly unidirectional wind shear, generated an environment favorable for severe organized convection.||Widely scattered strong to severe thunderstorms subsequently developed and tracked across the area during the late evening. The storms produced multiple reports of quarter-sized hail (one inch in diameter), including a report from a trained weather spotter in Beatrice, NE at 9:17 PM CST, and another from Emergency Management in Essex, IA at 10:27 PM CST.
episodes.212493: Ascent from a 700 mb shortwave within a broad plume of 1000-1500 J/kg of MLCAPE and 30-40 knots of effective shear supported development of thunderstorms on the afternoon of 4/14. Some of those became severe with reports of hail up to ping pong ball sized and uprooted trees from strong wind.
episodes.212505: A thunderstorm moving into Lake St. Clair produced a wind gust to 35 knots.
episodes.212506: A thunderstorm moving through western Lake Erie produced a wind gust of 45 knots.
episodes.212520: There was extensive river flooding along the Wisconsin River, Fox River, and Rock River in southern Wisconsin in April. The river levels were above normal after 5 inches of rain fell over the 5 days, and then another episode of heavy rain of 3 to 5 inches occurred on April 17th. In addition, vegetation was still fairly dormant so the grass was not able to soak up much of the rainfall.
episodes.212521: Clusters and broken lines of thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of 4/15 in Ohio and progressed east into the local area. Beneath a belt of enhanced mid-level flow, effective shear values reached 40-50 knots with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE in place. This supported swaths of straight-line wind damage with damage to trees, power lines, and structures as well as hail up to golf ball sized.
episodes.212547: During the morning and afternoon hours of April 15th, 2026, an upper-level wave ejected northward into the central Plains, pushing an attendant surface low pressure system from southeast Nebraska northeastward into central Iowa. This system pulled a warm sector northward into eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa, interacting with a weak convergent boundary draped generally along and just north of the Interstate 80 corridor. Driven by afternoon high temperatures peaking in the 70s, instability increased through the day, with a narrow ribbon of surface-based CAPE (SBCAPE) values exceeding 2,500 J/kg wrapping into the mid-Missouri River Valley. Under the influence of this unstable and highly sheared environment, two elevated severe supercells tracked across eastern Nebraska into southwest Iowa.||The first severe cell tracked generally from Schuyler, Nebraska, east-northeastward into Dunlap, Iowa. This storm produced several reports of quarter-sized (one inch in diameter) hail along its track. As the storm moved through Harrison County, Iowa, it intensified further, producing golf-ball-sized hail (1.75 inches in diameter) and wind-driven hail damage in Dunlap.||The second supercell developed northwest of Seward, Nebraska, and tracked northeastward to Wahoo, Nebraska, before gradually weakening as it approached the northern side of the Omaha metropolitan area. Notable severe reports from this storm included two-inch in diameter hail south-southwest of Dwight, Nebraska, and golf-ball-sized hail (1.75 inches in diameter) within Dwight itself, which resulted in visual damage to residential vinyl siding.
episodes.212548: During the morning and afternoon hours of April 15th, 2026, an upper-level wave ejected northward into the central Plains, pushing an attendant surface low pressure system from southeast Nebraska northeastward into central Iowa. This system pulled a warm sector northward into eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa, interacting with a weak convergent boundary draped generally along and just north of the Interstate 80 corridor. Driven by afternoon high temperatures peaking in the 70s, instability increased through the day, with a narrow ribbon of surface-based CAPE (SBCAPE) values exceeding 2,500 J/kg wrapping into the mid-Missouri River Valley. Under the influence of this unstable and highly sheared environment, two elevated severe supercells tracked across eastern Nebraska into southwest Iowa.||The first severe cell tracked generally from Schuyler, Nebraska, east-northeastward into Dunlap, Iowa. This storm produced several reports of quarter-sized (one inch in diameter) hail along its track. As the storm moved through Harrison County, Iowa, it intensified further, producing golf-ball-sized hail (1.75 inches in diameter) and wind-driven hail damage in Dunlap.
episodes.212624: Along a dryline, supercells initiated near Oklahoma/Kansas border. Some of these storms moved northward into Pratt and Barber counties. A social media post in Pratt county reported 1.5 inch hail.
episodes.212649: During the early morning hours of April 15th, an area of thunderstorms moved across Lake Erie and into far Western New York. The thunderstorms were associated with a weakening Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) tracking into the region from the west. The strong thunderstorms resulted in a 46 knot wind gust along the Lake Erie lakeshore near Westfield.
episodes.212825: The combination of an approaching front, a developing pre-frontal trough, and a mid-to upper-level trough promoted a moist and unstable weather pattern across the |region. This resulted in flooding, landslides, flash flooding and hail from April 12th to 15th.
episodes.212828: An area of thunderstorms moving out of Illinois intensified upon reaching north-central Indiana. Hail in excess of 2 inches in diameter was recorded along with at least one instance of damaging winds. Storms remained severe as they entered northwest Ohio.
episodes.212829: An area of thunderstorms moving out of Illinois intensified upon reaching north-central Indiana. Hail in excess of 2 inches in diameter was recorded along with at least one instance of damaging winds. Storms remained severe as they entered northwest Ohio.
episodes.212830: An area of thunderstorm moves across far southern Lower Michigan during the early morning hours of April 15th. A brief tornado has been confirmed south of Coldwater, MI with details outlined below. We wish to thank Branch County Emergency Management for their assistance with this survey.
episodes.212912: On Wednesday April 15th, a southwest flow pattern sent a mid-level shortwave disturbance into central NY, creating a favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. The combination of instability, strong wind shear, and ample moisture ultimately led to severe thunderstorms Wednesday afternoon and evening. The strongest storms produced estimated damaging wind gusts of 50 knots knocking down trees and wires.
episodes.212918: A marginally severe storm produced up to quarter size hail in Penalosa, Kansas the night of April 14th. No other reports were received.
episodes.212960: Multiple rounds of strong to severe storms impacted southeast Kansas during the afternoon and evening hours of April 15th. Storms produced up to golf ball sized hail and 70 mph wind gusts which blew over a semi truck in Montgomery County.
episodes.213000: Severe storms moved through lower Michigan late on the 14th into the early morning hours on the 15th. Very strong winds and 2 tornadoes occurred in the Grand Rapids forecast area. Total of 9 tornadoes were confirmed in Lower Michigan during this event.
episodes.213001: An active pattern led to multiple days worth of isolated to scattered severe thunderstorms across eastern New York. ||Within the warm sector of a low pressure system, sufficient destabilization and increased shear ahead of a prefrontal trough led to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms across eastern New York on April 14th. In the afternoon, discrete thunderstorms initially formed across portions of the Southern Adirondacks and shifted south and east into the Upper Hudson Valley. A few storms became severe, producing tree damage and subsequent traffic delays near Indian Lake, Warrensburg, and Lake Luzerne. Additionally, the Glens Falls ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph. Later in the afternoon and into the evening, the coverage of discrete cells increased, leading to clustering and the development of some more linear segments within the Capital Region and Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage resulted in the immediate Capital District near Clifton Park, Guilderland, Westmere, and Wyantskill from one linear storm that reached severe strength. Unfortunately, this storm was also responsible for an injury to a man in Wyantskill who was treated after a tree fell on top of him. In the evening, another linear cluster of storms tracked through portions of the eastern Catskills and into the lower Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage was subsequently reported near Kerhonkson and Amenia.||On April 15th, the cold front that proceeded the previous day's convection stalled near the region and became the source, in tandem with a decaying MCS from the Great Lakes, of additional scattered rain showers and isolated thunderstorms across the region. In particular, a cluster of thunderstorms became severe in the late evening of April 15th and caused fairly widespread tree damage throughout the Mid-Hudson Valley. Numerous trees were knocked down and blocked nearby roadways, causing temporary road closures or traffic delays. ||Finally, on April 16th, a compact shortwave trough moved towards the region while a surface disturbance tracked along the persistent boundary. Additional isolated to scattered thunderstorms tracked through the region, mainly in the late afternoon through evening hours. A couple of storms in particular became severe, causing widespread tree damage in a confined area of Fulton County and additionally produced 1 in diameter hail.
episodes.213006: Thunderstorms developed along a dryline and some of these storms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.213151: There were a few rounds of thunderstorms through this period. A few storms were severe with large hail and damaging winds and an isolated tornado.
episodes.213181: Heavy rainfall from multiple rounds of thunderstorms during the middle of April resulted in several area rivers reaching flood stage. Some rivers reached moderate to major flood stage, with the Lemonwier River at New Lisbon approaching its flood of record.

events.narrative: In Princeton, there were downed trees and wires near Ball Hill Rd.
Trained spotter estimates 70 MPH wind gusts.
Roadway flooding near the intersection of Gore Boulevard and 2nd Street in Lawton. The event time is estimated.
Public report of 1 inch diameter hail in Ripon.
Hail up to quarter-size about two-miles SSW of Plymouth.
Strong thunderstorms winds knocked a tree down on county route 116 near Lake Huntington.
In Holden, a tree was down on a house near Manning St.
In Lancaster, a tree was down on a house near Crescent St.
A parked bus was flipped over on State Route 47.
Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down wires on roadway.
Benjamin Logan Elementary School was damaged.
A tree fell onto County Road 26.
Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree on roadway.
Several trees were downed.
A few power poles were downed near the intersection of State Route 47 and County Road 12.
A roof was blown off of a barn.

Flash flooding of streets in southern Ozaukee County. More specifically, flooded roads and intersections on Mequon Rd. from Wauwatosa Rd. to just east of I-43. Other intersections  across the area with 3-6 inches of standing water.
A tree was downed across East Liberty Road near State Route 347.
Flash flooding of streets from Sussex toward Menomonee Falls.
Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree on roadway.
Tipton (TIPT) Mesonet observation.
Reported by a broadcast media storm chaser. The location is approximate.
Tipton (TIPT) Mesonet observation.
Power poles blown down just south of Stockton Illinois. This was determined to be done by straight line winds.

A tornado formed briefly in the occlusion of an rear flank downdraft northwest of Pearl City. It heavily damaged and destroyed several farm outbuildings, lifted a large farm wagon into an outbuilding, damaging the roof and side. The tornado also snapped several tree trunks and tree damage. Power poles were also snapped as the tornado crossed Illinois Highway 73 before lifting shortly thereafter. The tornado caused EF-1 damage with maximum estimated winds of 105 mph.
Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree on Wild Turnpike Road.
A local 911 Call Center relayed a report of a tree and wires down on Route 209 near Kyserike Road near Accord, NY.

Widespread wind damage in and east of Pearl City consistent with 80 to 95 mph. Damage was to trees, numerous snapped half way up and some uprooted, as well as some structural damage including a coffee trailer rolled. This damage appeared to be caused by the rear flank downdraft of the storm that produced a tornado just north of Pearl City.
Some street flooding in Germantown.

Flash flooding of streets and sidewalks mainly in northwest Milwaukee County, including stranded vehicles in floodwaters. Some reports of basement flooding in northern Milwaukee County. Pictures and videos provided.
Trained spotter reports broken tree branches and limbs.
A video of significant flash flooding of a creek with large debris was relayed by broadcast media.
Trained spotter estimates 70 MPH wind gusts.
Rainfall amounts of a little over an inch in a little over an hour caused closed roadways due to flash flooding in the city of Green Bay.
Rainfall amounts of 1 to 2 inches in a short period of time caused closed roadways due to flash flooding in Kewaunee and near Luxemburg.
Emergency management reported several roads washed out.

Emergency managers reported a landslide that damaged a house���s patio wall adjacent to PR-132 in Urb. Casamia, Barrio Canas, Ponce. Radar estimates indicate that approximately 2 to 2.5 inches of rain fell that afternoon in that area.

Heavy rain due to repeated rounds of thunderstorms during the middle of April resulted in the Lemonweir River at New Lisbon reaching flood stage during the evening hours on April 14th. The river crested in major flood stage and near the flood of record during the evening hours on April 16th before falling below flood stage during the afternoon on April 21st.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 70 mph that blew down a large, free-standing flagpole south of Carta Valley.
Three power poles were snapped along a portion of Lee Boulevard. The event time is estimated based on radar observations.
Numerous trees were downed along Peter Hoover Road.
NWS Albany received a report of large tree limbs down blocking one lane on NY-22 in Amenia via an email from NY Alert.
Illinois Highway 78 was closed for several hours due to water over the highway.
Several trees were downed at a property on State Route 310.
Several trees were downed and a part of a roof was blown off of a barn.
A photo was shared of a tree uprooted in Durand.

The tornado started northwest of County Road ES, west of Interstate 43, south of East Troy where it heavily damaged two barns.  Corn stubble was noted to be deposited from the corn field to the west all along a path through a cemetery up to Interstate 43.  Some tree damage was noted along Alpine Valley Golf Course.  The tornado then moved along County Road D and caused additional damage to some barns and outbuildings along with numerous trees.  The tornado ended somewhere south of County Road D and northwest of Valley View Road.
A tree fell onto power lines.
Several trees were downed near the intersection of Burg Street and New Burg Street.
The AWOS station KBPG Big Spring measured a 60 mph thunderstorm wind gust. The total time of occurrence is estimated.
Several trees were downed along Griffith Road. A barn and trailer were also damaged.
Law enforcement reported part of the road washed out with water over much of the road, resulting in closing the road off by barricade.
A tree fell onto a roadway.

The tornado developed northwest of Honey Creek Road and then hit a barn along the road, shifting it off of its foundation.  The tornado then continued southeast toward Waterford, removing sheet metal from a shed along Buena Park Rd. The tornado then continued through the north side and downtown Waterford where most of the damage was to trees and houses from the trees falling on them.  A few trees were noted to have been lofted and dropped into the Fox River.  The tornado then continued through the east side of Waterford before ending near Highway 36.
Trained spotter reports uprooted trees and shingle damage from thunderstorm winds.
Sporadic damage path along Plank Road with mainly tree damage.  Some barn/outbuildings had damage to their roofs with sheet metal panels missing/lofted in 2 locations.
A tree was downed along Poplar Grove Rd south of Poplar Grove.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 70 mph that peeled sheets of corrugated metal off the roof and walls of an unused hangar at the Edwards County Airport.

The tornado began northwest of Somers, east of Interstate 94.  It went through the north and east side of the city, through the fire department and near Somers Elementary School.  Numerous trees were uprooted along the path, some falling into houses.
A wind gust of 39 knots (45 MPH) was measured by a private weather station (KMDBALTI558) adjacent to the tidal Patapsco River.
A social media report of 1.5 inch hail.
The public reported quarter sized hail 4 miles south of Gillingham.
A wind gust of 43 knots (49 MPH) was measured by the I-695 Francis Scott Key Bridge NOS sensor (FSKM2).
Standing water was reported along Auburn St east of Auburn High School in Rockford.

This is the first segment of a two-segment tornado. The tornado developed south of W 81st Street S and just west of S 39th West Avenue. The tornado moved east-northeast damaging the roofs of several homes, some severely, destroying outbuildings, snapping or uprooting numerous trees, and snapping power poles before it crossed into Tulsa County near W 81st Street S. The tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KINX WSR-88D. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in this segment of the tornado was 100 to 110 mph.

This is the second segment of a two-segment tornado. The tornado crossed into Tulsa County near W 81st Street S. In Tulsa County, the tornado damaged several homes, uprooted numerous trees, snapped the trunks of some trees, and blew down power lines until it dissipated near Highway 75, north of W 78th Street S. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in this segment of the tornado was 95 to 105 mph.

At least two vehicles were stuck in flood waters on Weathersfield Way near Schaumburg.  A vehicle was disabled in flood waters on Busse Road under the Interstate 90 bridge.  Four cars were stuck in flood waters at the intersection of Roselle Road and Wise Road.  Street and viaduct flooding was reported in Des Plaines and Mount Prospect.  At least one basement flooded in Schaumburg and at least two basements flooded in Mount Prospect.  Rainfall amounts included 2.63 inches in Mount Prospect; 2.62 inches two miles east of Schaumburg and 2.10 inches in Elk Grove Village.

events.narrative: An EF-0 tornado with peak winds estimated near 80 mph. The tornado began near Schermerhorn Lake in Allegan County and was on the ground for around 6.5 miles before lifting west/northwest of Otsego.
Trees were reported down near Grand River Road and Delaney Road.

Widespread tree damage occurred along the tornado path. Several large barns were heavily damaged and multiple homes and businesses lost roofing material or were |damaged by fallen trees. Debris from one business landed on US-131|forcing it to be closed for a period of time following the tornado. The tornado continued into Barry County.

The tornado started in a field on northwest side of W Birch Run Rd and|Amman Rd. It first produced EF-0 damage with two rows of pine trees|uprooted, along with removing siding from an outbuilding.  The tornado|then continued northeast toward Fergus Rd and Gasper Rd where more pine|trees were uprooted.  EF-1 damage occurred on a half mile stretch of|Bishop Rd with the greatest concentration of EF-1 damage near Bishop Rd|and Alicia Rd.  Peak winds estimated at 95 mph. This damage included both pine and hardwood trees snapped, two outbuildings and a few empty silos destroyed, along with three homes that sustained roof damage.  One home did have the majority of the roof|blown off with the attached garage walls blown out.  It continued east producing EF-0 damage to an outbuilding northeast of Alicia Rd and Horning Cut Rd where a door and wall were collapsed before lifting just off on an outbuilding.  The tornado then lifted just off to the northeast in a field.

This tornado developed just east of Highway 69, northeast of Summit, where trees were uprooted, homes were damaged, and power poles were snapped. The tornado moved northeast across Highway 64, damaging numerous homes, snapping and uprooting trees, and snapping power poles. It then crossed Highway 351 and turned to the east along Hancock Street, before crossing the Arkansas River and dissipating east of Highway 10. A few trees were uprooted and numerous large tree limbs were snapped in the path east of Highway 351. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 100 to 110 mph.

The tornado touched down near Newburg Rd just west of Lansing Rd before moving|east across Lansing Rd. EF-0 damage occurred along the path with downed pine|trees and large tree limbs.  Some structural damage was seen with siding off|of a home, outbuilding roof panels blown off and collapsed barn doors near|Newburg Rd and Vernon Rd. Peak winds estimated at 80 mph.  The tornado lifted just to the southeast of Newburg Rd and S Reed Rd where there were both downed hardwood and pine trees, along with large tree limbs.

Widespread street and basement flooding was reported across much of northern Chicago, including Edison Park, Norwood Park, Jefferson Park, Rogers Park, Edgewater, Uptown, Forest Glen, North Park and West Ridge. Lakeshore Drive was flooded near Montrose Beach. The underpass on Interstate 94 at Pratt Avenue in Lincolnwood was flooded. In Edison Park, cars were reported stalled with water up to their bumpers.  Multiple roads and viaducts were flooded in Rosemont and near O'Hare Airport, including along portions of Interstate 90.  Rainfall amounts included 3.46 inches in Harwood Heights; 2.66 inches in Rogers Park; 2.59 inches in Park Ridge and 2.56 inches in Lincolnwood. Chicago O'Hare Airport measured 2.43 inches, which was a record 24 hour total for April 14th.

This is the first segment of a three-segment tornado. The tornado developed south of Highway 51, southeast of Eldon, where numerous large tree limbs were snapped.  It moved northeast into Adair County, south of the 754 Road. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in this segment of the tornado was 80 to 85 mph.

This is the second segment of a three-segment tornado. The tornado moved into Adair County south of the 754 Road, and into rugged terrain. Trees were uprooted as it moved across the 4630 Roads southwest of Christie, and the roof of a manufactured home was damaged. The tornado uprooted numerous trees and snapped numerous large tree limbs along Highway 62, with more trees uprooted along Cemetery Road and Highway 59, and along the 4750 Road before moving into Washington County, AR. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in this segment of the tornado was 90 to 100 mph.

This is the first segment of a two-segment tornado. The tornado developed just west of Piney Road, south of the 782 Road, where trees were uprooted. The tornado moved northeast uprooting trees along Piney Road and the 4765 Road, before crossing into Washington County, AR. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in this segment of the tornado was 90 to 100 mph.

This is the third segment of a three-segment tornado. The tornado moved into Washington County, AR, south of W Cincinnati Road. It moved northeast across Highway 59 near Cincinnati, where numerous large tree limbs were snapped. Numerous large tree limbs were also snapped as it crossed Rennic Road and Ham Road before dissipating. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in this segment of the tornado was 75 to 85 mph.

This is the second segment of a two-segment tornado. The tornado crossed into Washington County, AR, near the 4765 Road. It crossed the Baron Fork River, and damaged outbuildings, uprooted trees, and snapped numerous large tree limbs along Salem Springs Road. Trees were uprooted or snapped along Highway 59 and Sugar Hill Road, before the tornado dissipated southwest of Lincoln. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in this segment of the tornado was 95 to 105 mph.

A survey of damage south of Coldwater Michigan indicates that a circulation may have attempted to touch down on Sanford Rd, north of Fenn Road where a barn suffered damage with debris thrown to the east, impacting portions of a solar farm with some damage to panels. A few tree tops showed some minor damage from Sanford Rd|to near Interstate 69 where it appears the circulation finally touched down at a business on the southeast side of the Interstate, causing damage to a pole barn on the property. It continued southeast causing tree damage until reaching the area of|Dubendorf and Quimby Road where a garage lost its roof, trees were blown down and vinyl fencing around a pool was blown down. The tornado then impacted a pole barn on South Wood Rd, throwing the debris well east into the field before lifting. Maximum wind speeds were estimated in the 85 to 90 mph range.

A swath of severe straight-line convective wind gusts affected Brookfield Township. Damage was observed along Everett East Road from west of County Route 167 to Greensleaves Circle East. Along Everett East Road, winds lifted a trampoline from a|backyard, deposited it in the front yard of a nearby residence, and blew down a fence. In the Trumbull County Metroparks, on the north side of Everett East Road, approximately 30 to 40 trees were downed, all oriented toward the southeast. Several healthy trees were snapped at their bases, supporting higher-end wind estimates. A large tree was downed on the north side of Everett East Road, clipped a home, and damaged the roof. Additionally, several large tree limbs fell onto two homes and caused minor structural damage. Other trees were downed on the south side of Everett East Road.||All observed tree damage and debris were consistently oriented toward the southeast, indicating straight-line wind damage from a microburst since the corridor of damage appeared to have a maximum width of 250 yards. Maximum wind gusts were estimated to have been 90-mph.
